Sloane\\n\\nMathematics\\n\\nNumber Theory\\n\\nA base-b junction number u has the property that there are at least two ways to write it as u = v + s(v), where s(v) is the sum of the digits in the expansion of the number v in base b. For the base-10 case, Kaprekar in the 1950's and 1960's studied the problem of finding K(n), the smallest u such that the equation u=v+s(v) has exactly n solutions. He gave the values K(2)=101, K(3)=10^13+1, and conjectured that K(4)=10^24+102. In 1966 Narasinga Rao gave the upper bound 10^1111111111124+102 for K(5), as well as upper bounds for K(6), K(7), K(8), and K(16). In the present work, we derive a set of recurrences which determine K(n) for any base b and in particular imply that these conjectured values of K(n) are correct. The key to our approach is an apparently new recurrence for F(u), the number of solutions to u=v+s(v). We illustrate our method by computing the values of K(n) for n <= 16 and bases b <= 10, and show that for each base K(n) grows as a tower of height proportional to log_2(n). Rearrange the digits to make the largest and smallest 4-digit numbers possible. Subtract the smaller number from the larger. Use the resulting number and repeat the process. For example, starting with 4,731: 7,431 − 1,347 = 6,084; 8,640 − 468 = 8,172; 8,721 − 1,278 = 7,443; 7,443 − 3,447 = 3,996; 9,963 − 3,699 = 6,264; 6,642 − 2,466 = 4,176; 7,641 − 1,467 = 6,174.
